claims.claim: ⚠️ **Early symptoms may be minimal; severe toxicity may only become apparent at 6–12 hours.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Serum concentration correlates poorly with toxicity; deterioration can occur as the serum level falls**, because CNS concentration is rising.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Classic acute features:** tinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hidden sources:** aspirin-containing compounds · **oil of wintergreen (1 teaspoon of 98% salicylate = 7000 mg)** · willow bark · Dencorub · some teething gels.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Under 150 mg/kg:** symptoms minimal. **150–300 mg/kg:** mild to moderate (tinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation). ⚠️ **Over 300 mg/kg: severe (acidosis, seizures, hyperthermia).**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hyperventilation is not always present in children — its absence does not exclude significant toxicity.** Assess dehydration carefully.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **History:** dose and time, immediate- or sustained-release product, co-ingestants, and whether accidental or intentional.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Blood gases indicate severity:** phase 1: respiratory alkalosis plus alkaluria → phase 2: respiratory alkalosis plus paradoxical aciduria (pH under 6) → **phase 3 metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Salicylate level at presentation, then every 2–4 hours until falling if the child is symptomatic or the product enteric-coated.** Also U&E, creatinine and glucose.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat (and admit/consult):** acute ingestion of 150 mg/kg or more · all symptomatic patients · unknown quantity.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Intubation apnoea can worsen acidosis and cause cardiac arrest.** Get senior help, and consider sodium bicarbonate pre-loading. **If ventilated, keep pH 7.45–7.5** — which may mean matching the pre-intubation respiratory rate.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Activated charcoal 1 g/kg**, ideally within 1 hour, may be indicated after a massive overdose — **discuss with toxicology (13 11 26) first.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rehydrate to euvolaemia; correct electrolytes and hypoglycaemia.** ⚠️ **Correct the metabolic acidosis — this is critical for limiting CNS penetration.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urinary alkalinisation: slow IV bicarbonate bolus 2 mmol/kg, then infusion 1 mmol/kg/hr, keeping urine pH above 7.5.** Needs a catheter to monitor urine pH. For mild–moderate salicylism.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Alkalinisation is not possible with hypokalaemia and itself causes urinary potassium loss — replace potassium IV to keep a mid-range level.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider haemodialysis early in moderate–severe poisoning.** Indications include: alkalinisation not feasible (renal failure, pulmonary oedema) · **level over 7.2 mmol/L (100 mg/dL), or a level climbing past 4.4 mmol/L (60 mg/dL) even with alkalinisation** · renal failure, altered mental state, hyperthermia over 39 °C despite cooling, or refractory acidaemia or electrolyte imbalance.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge after 6 hours' observation** if still asymptomatic with normal acid–base status and a level in the therapeutic range.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Refer to an ICU that can provide haemodialysis** if symptomatic after more than 300 mg/kg and/or meeting dialysis criteria. **PIPER: 1300 137 650.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intentional self-harm → local mental health services** (e.g. Orygen 1800 888 320); **recreational → YoDAA** (1800 458 685).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Salicylates poisoning' (Last updated June 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Salicylates_Posioning/, retrieved 2026-09-23
